title: insecure-cookie.set-secure-false
description: Cookie.setSecure(false) disables the Secure flag, allowing the cookie to be sent over cleartext HTTP (CWE-614). Call setSecure(true) for sensitive cookies.

title: Path traversal via attacker-controlled cookie value
description: The cookie value is taken from the request (attacker-controlled) and used directly in constructing a file path by concatenation. No validation, sanitization, or normalization is performed to prevent path traversal sequences like '../'. An attacker can supply a cookie value containing path traversal characters to read arbitrary files outside the intended directory.

title: Path Traversal via Unvalidated Cookie Value in FileOutputStream
description: The doPost method reads the cookie 'BenchmarkTest00002' from the request and uses its value (after URL decoding) to construct a file path by concatenating it with a base directory. The user-controlled cookie value is not validated or sanitized, allowing an attacker to supply path traversal sequences (e.g., '../../etc/passwd') to write to arbitrary files on the server. This is a classic path traversal vulnerability (CWE-22).

title: Cookie Domain Set from Host Header (Cookie Injection)
description: The cookie domain is set using the host obtained from request.getRequestURL(), which is derived from the HTTP Host header. An attacker can manipulate the Host header to control the cookie's domain attribute, potentially causing the cookie to be sent to an attacker-controlled domain. This can lead to session fixation, cookie theft, or unintended disclosure of cookie values. Although the cookie value in this specific test is hardcoded and non-sensitive, the vulnerable pattern is present.

title: Sensitive File Path Leaked via Console Output
description: When a FileOutputStream fails to open, the constructed file path (which includes user-controlled input) is printed to standard output. In production environments, stdout/stderr often end up in log files that may be accessible to attackers, leaking internal file system layout and potentially confirming the presence of path traversal vulnerabilities.

title: User-controlled cookie value used as session attribute key without validation
description: The param variable is derived from a cookie value without validation and used directly as the key for setting a session attribute. An attacker can control which session attribute is set by providing a crafted cookie. While the value is fixed to "10340", this could allow overwriting existing session attributes that may be used for security decisions (e.g., authentication state, roles). This constitutes a trust boundary violation.

title: Use of broken or risky cryptographic algorithm DES
description: The code uses DES, which is a deprecated algorithm with a 56-bit key that can be brute-forced with modern hardware. Even though the key is randomly generated each time, the algorithm itself is considered broken and provides insufficient confidentiality protection. An attacker who obtains the ciphertext (stored in passwordFile.txt) could recover the plaintext with moderate effort.

title: Information exposure through stack trace in HTTP response
description: The catch block writes the full stack trace of the exception to the HTTP response via e.printStackTrace(response.getWriter()). This exposes internal implementation details such as class names, method names, line numbers, and potentially sensitive system paths to the client, aiding an attacker in understanding the application's internals and crafting further attacks.

title: Unhandled IllegalArgumentException from URLDecoder.decode leading to potential information disclosure or denial of service
description: The call to java.net.URLDecoder.decode(param, "UTF-8") can throw IllegalArgumentException if the input string contains malformed percent-encoding (e.g., "%ZZ" or incomplete "%X"). This exception is not caught by any try-catch block (the surrounding try block starts at line 62, after this decode), so it propagates to the servlet container. The container may return an error response that includes a stack trace, leaking internal information, or it may cause a denial of service if the exception disrupts request handling. An attacker can trigger this by sending a specially crafted header value.

title: SQL Injection in stored procedure call via user-controlled header
description: The code directly concatenates the user-supplied HTTP header 'BenchmarkTest00008' (after URL decoding) into a SQL stored procedure call string. An attacker can control the header value and inject arbitrary SQL commands by crafting input that breaks out of the intended call syntax. This allows reading, modifying, or deleting database records outside the intended query.

title: Missing input size validation on attacker-controlled header name leads to potential denial of service (CPU exhaustion) when used as input to hash function.
description: The servlet takes the first non-standard HTTP header name as input ('param') and uses it directly as the source for a SHA-384 hash computation. No validation or size limitation is applied to the header name. An attacker can send a request with an arbitrarily long header name (e.g., several megabytes) to force the server to allocate memory for the byte array and spend CPU time hashing the input, potentially causing a denial-of-service condition through resource exhaustion. The code also does not close the FileWriter in a finally block (resource leak), but that is not a security issue. The primary concern is uncontrolled resource consumption triggered by an unvalidated external input.

title: Weak random number range used for remember-me token (only 99 possible values)
description: The remember-me key is generated by SecureRandom.nextInt(99), which produces a value between 0 and 98. An attacker can trivially brute-force all 99 possible values to forge a valid cookie and impersonate any user who has been remembered. Although SecureRandom is cryptographically strong, the tiny output space defeats its purpose.

title: Path traversal vulnerability in file path construction from user-controlled HTTP header
description: The HTTP request header 'BenchmarkTest00011' is directly used as the parent directory parameter in a java.io.File constructor after URL decoding. An attacker can control this header to traverse directories (e.g., using '../' sequences or absolute paths), allowing them to reference arbitrary files on the server's filesystem. The subsequent existence check and response message disclose whether the targeted file exists, enabling information gathering about the file system layout.

title: LDAP Injection via unsanitized header value in LDAP filter
description: The servlet reads the 'BenchmarkTest00012' HTTP header, URL-decodes it, and concatenates it directly into an LDAP search filter string on line 60 without any escaping or validation. The filter is then passed to InitialDirContext.search() on line 68. An attacker can inject LDAP special characters (e.g., ')' or '*') to alter the filter logic, potentially bypassing access controls, enumerating entries, or extracting sensitive information from the LDAP directory. The use of ESAPI encoding for output does not mitigate injection at the query level.

title: Externally-Controlled Format String (Format String Injection)
description: The 'Referer' HTTP header is user-controlled input. It is URL-decoded and then directly used as the format string in a call to `response.getWriter().format()`. An attacker can supply format specifiers (e.g., `%s`, `%x`, `%n`, `%9999999d`) to cause information disclosure, excessive memory consumption, or denial of service. Although Java format strings are less dangerous than C's, they can still leak internal values through argument indexing and produce unbounded output.

title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via reflected Referer header
description: The 'Referer' HTTP header is read, URL-decoded, and then written directly into the HTTP response via `response.getWriter().format(param, obj)` without any HTML encoding or sanitization. Since the response content type is `text/html`, any HTML or JavaScript embedded in the header value will be interpreted by the browser, leading to reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS). Additionally, the `X-XSS-Protection` header is explicitly set to '0', disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter, which makes exploitation easier.

title: Command Injection in ProcessBuilder shell command
description: The HTTP header 'BenchmarkTest00015' is user-controlled. Its value is URL-decoded and then concatenated directly into a shell command string 'echo ' + param. The command is passed to cmd.exe /c or sh -c, causing it to be interpreted by a shell. An attacker can inject arbitrary OS commands by including shell metacharacters (e.g., ;, |, &, `, $()) in the header value. This results in OS command injection.

title: OS Command Injection via HTTP header
description: The servlet reads the 'BenchmarkTest00017' HTTP header value and passes it unsanitized and unvalidated directly to Runtime.exec(). An attacker can inject arbitrary OS commands by crafting a malicious header. The command output is also returned to the attacker via printOSCommandResults(), making the injection both exploitable and visible. On non-Windows systems the cmd variable remains empty, so the entire header value is executed as a command. On Windows, although a prefix is added, the attacker can still inject additional commands through shell metacharacters or by manipulating the program name.

title: SQL Injection via unsanitized header value concatenated into SQL query
description: The servlet reads a value from the HTTP header 'BenchmarkTest00018', URL-decodes it, and directly concatenates it into a SQL INSERT statement without any sanitization, parameterization, or escaping. An attacker can control the header value to inject arbitrary SQL commands, breaking out of the string literal context and executing malicious SQL (e.g., inserting rogue admin users, modifying or deleting data). The executeUpdate() call then sends this unsanitized SQL to the database.

title: DES is a cryptographically broken algorithm due to its 56-bit key size, which can be brute-forced with modern hardware.
description: The code uses KeyGenerator.getInstance("DES") to generate a secret key for encryption. DES uses a 56-bit key, which is considered insecure against modern brute-force attacks. Even if the actual cipher algorithm loaded from benchmark.properties defaults to DESede (Triple-DES), the key generated here is a DES key, which may be insufficient for the intended algorithm and represents weak cryptographic practice.

title: ECB mode is insecure for encrypting data because identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking data patterns and structure.
description: The cipher algorithm defaults to "DESede/ECB/PKCS5Padding" and is fetched from application properties. ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode does not use an initialization vector and encrypts each block independently, meaning identical input blocks produce identical output blocks. This makes the ciphertext vulnerable to pattern analysis, block replay, and plaintext recovery attacks. ECB is well-documented as an insecure mode of operation.

title: Exception stack traces are written directly to the HTTP response, exposing internal implementation details to the client.
description: When a cryptographic exception occurs (NoSuchAlgorithmException, NoSuchPaddingException, etc.), the code calls e.printStackTrace(response.getWriter()), which writes the full stack trace including class names, method names, file names, and line numbers to the HTTP response output. This information disclosure aids attackers in fingerprinting the application and understanding its internal structure, potentially revealing attack surfaces.

title: Use of weak cryptographic algorithm DES
description: The code uses DES (Data Encryption Standard) for encryption, which is a 56-bit symmetric cipher considered cryptographically weak and deprecated. DES is vulnerable to brute-force attacks (can be broken in under 24 hours with dedicated hardware) and should not be used for any security-sensitive operation. The use of DES/CBC without authentication also makes the system potentially vulnerable to padding oracle attacks if the ciphertext is later decrypted and validated.

title: Information exposure via stack trace in HTTP response
description: In multiple exception handlers, the full stack trace is written directly to the HTTP response via e.printStackTrace(response.getWriter()). This leaks internal implementation details, class names, method names, file paths, and potentially sensitive data (such as parts of keys or configuration) to the client, aiding attackers in crafting further exploits.

title: LDAP Injection via unsanitized user input concatenated into LDAP filter
description: The servlet retrieves the 'BenchmarkTest00021' parameter from the HTTP request and directly concatenates it into an LDAP filter string without any sanitization, escaping, or validation. An attacker can inject arbitrary LDAP filter syntax (e.g., closing the active filter and adding new conditions) to manipulate the query, potentially bypassing access controls, enumerating data, or performing blind LDAP injection attacks.

title: Use of java.util.Random for security-sensitive remember-me key generation
description: The code uses java.util.Random.nextFloat() to generate the remember-me cookie key. java.util.Random is a weak PRNG that is not cryptographically secure. It can be easily predicted if an attacker observes a few outputs, allowing them to forge a valid remember-me cookie and impersonate any user. The generated key is used as the sole authentication credential in the cookie-based 'remember me' mechanism (lines 65, 82).

title: Cookie domain derived from user-controllable Host header
description: The cookie domain is set by parsing the request URL (which reflects the Host header sent by the client) and extracting the host component. An attacker can control the Host header (e.g., via a malicious request or a proxy that forwards the Host header) and cause the cookie to be set for an attacker-chosen domain. This can lead to cookie injection or session fixation across domains.

title: Remember-me key exposed in HTTP response body
description: The generated remember-me key (the cookie value) is written to the HTTP response body. This exposes the secret key to any intermediate proxies, caches, or browser extensions that can read the response. An attacker who obtains this key can forge the cookie and impersonate the user.

title: SQL Injection via string concatenation in SQL query
description: The parameter 'param' from request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest00024") is directly concatenated into the SQL string without any sanitization or parameterization. Although a PreparedStatement is used, only the first placeholder (USERNAME=?) is bound via setString(1, "foo"), while the password part is built via string concatenation. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL by providing a malicious value in the 'BenchmarkTest00024' parameter, leading to authentication bypass, data leakage, or data manipulation.

title: SQL Injection through unsanitized user input in SQL query concatenation
description: The servlet retrieves the request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00025' without any validation or sanitization and directly concatenates it into a SQL query string. An attacker can control the 'param' value to inject arbitrary SQL commands, enabling authentication bypass, data exfiltration, or other malicious actions. The use of Spring's JDBCtemplate.queryForObject with a raw string does not prevent injection because the query is built via string concatenation rather than using parameterized queries or prepared statements.

title: SQL Injection via string concatenation in query
description: The servlet directly concatenates the user-controlled request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00026' into a SQL query string without any sanitization, parameterization, or escaping. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL commands, potentially leading to authentication bypass, data leakage, data modification, or complete database compromise.

title: SQL Injection in INSERT statement via direct string concatenation of user input
description: The servlet retrieves the 'BenchmarkTest00027' HTTP request parameter (line 44) and directly concatenates it into an SQL INSERT statement (line 47). The resulting SQL string is executed via a Statement.executeUpdate() call (line 52). No input validation, escaping, or parameterized query (PreparedStatement) is used, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL commands by crafting a malicious parameter value. For example, a value like "'||(SELECT ...)||'" or a closing quote followed by additional SQL statements could be injected to manipulate the query.

title: Path Traversal leading to arbitrary file write
description: The servlet retrieves a user-controlled parameter 'BenchmarkTest00028' (line 47) and concatenates it directly with a base directory path (line 55) to form a file path, which is then used to open a FileOutputStream (line 57). No validation, sanitization, or path traversal prevention is applied to the user input. An attacker can supply a value such as '../../etc/passwd' to write to an arbitrary location on the filesystem, leading to potential denial of service, data corruption, or remote code execution if a writeable location like a web directory or cron script is targeted.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via user-controlled format string in printf
description: The servlet retrieves a user-controlled parameter 'BenchmarkTest00030' and directly passes it as the format string to response.getWriter().printf() without any validation, sanitization, or encoding. The output is written to an HTML response (content-type text/html). An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML or JavaScript, leading to reflected XSS. Additionally, the X-XSS-Protection header is set to '0', which disables the browser's built-in XSS filter, making exploitation easier. The printf call also exposes a format string injection vector: an attacker can supply format specifiers (e.g., %s, %n) that may cause exceptions (MissingFormatArgumentException) or leak information through error messages, though the primary impact is XSS.

title: User-controlled input stored as session 'userid' without validation allows session poisoning and identity impersonation.
description: The servlet retrieves the request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00031' and stores it directly as the session attribute 'userid' via HttpSession.putValue(). The 'userid' attribute is typically relied upon by the application for authentication and authorization decisions. Because the value originates from the HTTP request without any server-side validation or authentication check, an attacker can arbitrarily set this session value to impersonate any user (e.g., 'admin', 'manager', or another user ID). This violates the trust boundary between client-supplied data and server-side security context, potentially allowing privilege escalation and unauthorized access.

title: SQL Injection via string concatenation in SQL query
description: The user-supplied parameter 'param' is directly concatenated into a SQL query string without any sanitization, parameterization, or escaping. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL commands by crafting a malicious input (e.g., setting param to "' OR '1'='1"). The query is then executed via Spring's JDBCtemplate.execute(), which does not protect against injection when passed a concatenated string. Although the output is HTML-encoded for display, the injection occurs at the database layer before any encoding happens.

title: SQL Injection via string concatenation in SQL query
description: The user-supplied parameter 'param' is directly concatenated into a SQL query string without any sanitization, parameterization, or escaping. An attacker can control the 'BenchmarkTest00033' request parameter to inject arbitrary SQL commands, potentially bypassing authentication, extracting sensitive data, or performing other database operations.

title: SQL Injection via string concatenation of user-controlled parameter
description: The parameter 'param' is obtained directly from the HTTP request parameter map without any sanitization or validation. It is concatenated directly into a SQL query string, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL commands. This is a classic SQL injection vulnerability, as the input is not parameterized or escaped.

title: Stack trace exposed in HTTP response
description: The catch block on line 118 calls e.printStackTrace(response.getWriter()), which outputs the full exception stack trace directly to the HTTP response. This exposes internal implementation details such as class names, method names, file paths, and line numbers to the client. An attacker can use this information to gain insight into the application's structure and craft further attacks.

title: Use of weak cryptographic algorithm DES
description: The code uses DES (Data Encryption Standard) for key generation, which uses a 56-bit key. DES is considered cryptographically weak and can be brute-forced with modern hardware. NIST has deprecated DES. This directly undermines the confidentiality of the encrypted data.

title: Use of insecure ECB encryption mode
description: The default algorithm specified uses ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode. ECB mode encrypts each plaintext block independently, making it deterministic and leaking patterns in the plaintext. This allows an attacker to infer information about the encrypted data, especially when the same plaintext block appears multiple times. ECB is considered insecure for general-purpose encryption.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via unencoded user-controlled parameter name written to HTML response
description: The servlet retrieves a user-controlled HTTP parameter name (where the corresponding value equals 'BenchmarkTest00036') and writes that name directly into the HTML response without any encoding or sanitization. The response content type is set to 'text/html', so the browser will interpret the output as HTML. An attacker can supply a parameter name containing malicious JavaScript (e.g., <script>alert(1)</script>) with a value of 'BenchmarkTest00036', and the attacker-controlled name will be reflected in the response and executed in the victim's browser. Additionally, the code explicitly disables the browser's built-in XSS filter by setting the 'X-XSS-Protection' header to '0', making exploitation easier.

title: SQL Injection via concatenation of user-controlled parameter name into SQL query
description: The parameter `param` is derived from the name of an HTTP request parameter (line 54) where the corresponding value equals 'BenchmarkTest00037'. This value is directly concatenated into the SQL query string on line 61 using string concatenation, even though a PreparedStatement is used. The PreparedStatement parameter placeholder is only used for the USERNAME field (set to 'foo'), but the PASSWORD field includes the unsanitized `param` value. An attacker can control the parameter name, allowing them to inject arbitrary SQL syntax into the query, leading to SQL injection.

title: SQL Injection via concatenated parameter name
description: The servlet retrieves a parameter name from the HTTP request (line 54) and directly concatenates it into a SQL query string (line 61) without any sanitization or parameterization. The 'param' value originates from request.getParameterNames() (line 46) and is selected when any parameter value equals 'BenchmarkTest00038'. An attacker can control the parameter name and inject arbitrary SQL by providing a malicious parameter name. The query is executed via Spring's JdbcTemplate.query() without using prepared statements or parameter placeholders, making it vulnerable to SQL injection.

title: SQL Injection via parameter name concatenated into SQL query
description: The code extracts a parameter name from the HTTP request (the name whose value equals "BenchmarkTest00039") and directly concatenates it into a SQL query string without any sanitization or parameterization. An attacker can control the parameter name by simply crafting a request where a parameter's value is "BenchmarkTest00039" and the parameter name contains SQL injection payloads, e.g., `foo' OR '1'='1`. This allows the attacker to manipulate the query logic, potentially bypass authentication or extract arbitrary data from the database.

title: Path Traversal - Arbitrary file path used to construct File object from user-controlled input
description: The servlet retrieves the 'BenchmarkTest00040' request parameter (line 46) and passes it directly as the argument to the java.io.File constructor (line 49) without any validation, sanitization, or restriction on the path. This allows an attacker to control the file path used on the server's filesystem. Additionally, the code exposes a file existence oracle (lines 59-63) by telling the attacker whether the specified file exists, which can be used to probe the filesystem. Although ESAPI encoding is used for HTML output, it does not mitigate path traversal.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via unsanitized user input
description: The servlet retrieves the 'BenchmarkTest00041' parameter from the HTTP request and writes it directly to the HTTP response without any HTML encoding or sanitization. The response content type is set to 'text/html', so the browser will interpret the output as HTML. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript by crafting a malicious parameter value. Additionally, the X-XSS-Protection header is set to '0', which disables the browser's built-in XSS filter, making exploitation easier.

title: X-XSS-Protection header disabled
description: The application explicitly sets the X-XSS-Protection header to '0', which disables the browser's built-in reflective XSS filter. While this header is considered obsolete and not relied upon by modern browsers, it still reduces the defense-in-depth for legacy browsers. Combined with the reflective XSS vulnerability, this setting increases the risk.

title: Weak randomness for remember-me token using SecureRandom.nextInt() (32-bit entropy)
description: The code uses SecureRandom.nextInt() to generate a remember-me token, which returns a 32-bit signed integer. Converting this to a string via Integer.toString(r) yields only 32 bits of entropy. For a security-sensitive token used to identify a user session, this low entropy makes the token susceptible to brute-force attacks. An attacker who can observe or guess the token pattern could forge a valid remember-me cookie and impersonate a user.

title: Sensitive token exposed in HTTP response body
description: The remember-me token (rememberMeKey) is printed directly into the HTTP response body. This exposes the token to anyone who can observe the response, including network intermediaries, browser history, proxy logs, server logs, and any cross-site scripting vulnerabilities on the same origin. An attacker who obtains this token can impersonate the user.

title: Missing authentication before granting access
description: The servlet does not perform any authentication or authorization check. It automatically assigns a hardcoded username 'SafeIngrid' (appended with a test case number) and issues a remember-me cookie without verifying the user's identity. This effectively allows any unauthenticated visitor to be recognized as that user. While the cookie token is random, the lack of a login step means the endpoint cannot distinguish between legitimate users and attackers.

title: SQL Injection via string concatenation in INSERT statement
description: The parameter 'param' is obtained directly from the HTTP request via scr.getTheParameter("BenchmarkTest00043") without any sanitization, escaping, or validation (beyond a null check). This value is directly concatenated into a SQL INSERT statement on line 49. The resulting string is then executed as a SQL statement via Statement.executeUpdate() on line 54. An attacker can control the 'BenchmarkTest00043' parameter to inject arbitrary SQL commands, potentially modifying or extracting data from the database, or performing other malicious operations.

title: LDAP Injection via unsanitized user input in search filter
description: The user-supplied parameter `param` (obtained from request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00044') is directly concatenated into an LDAP search filter string on line 56 without any sanitization or encoding. An attacker can inject LDAP metacharacters such as `)`, `(`, `*`, `|`, `&`, `!`, etc., to modify the logical structure of the query. For example, supplying `*)(uid=*))` would produce the filter `(&(objectclass=person)(uid=*)(uid=*)))`, which returns all user entries, bypassing any intended restriction. This is a classic LDAP injection vulnerability (CWE-90). Although ESAPI is used for HTML-encoding output (mitigating XSS), no LDAP-specific escaping is applied to the filter itself.

title: Path traversal vulnerability in file access
description: The HTTP request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00045' is taken directly from the user and concatenated with a base directory path to form a file name. No validation or sanitization (e.g., path traversal filtering) is applied to the user-supplied value. An attacker can include '../' sequences or absolute path components to read or write arbitrary files on the server filesystem outside the intended directory. The file is then opened for both reading (via FileInputStream) and writing (via FileOutputStream), which could lead to unauthorized file access, data leakage, or file corruption.

title: Use of weak cryptographic hash algorithm MD5 for security-sensitive hashing
description: The code uses MD5, a cryptographically broken hash algorithm, to hash user-controlled input and stores the result in a password file (passwordFile.txt). MD5 is vulnerable to collision attacks and should not be used for any security-related purpose such as password storage or integrity verification. The context suggests the hash is intended for security-sensitive use (storing in a 'passwordFile'), making this a significant weakness.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via unsanitized query parameter used in format output
description: The servlet extracts the value of the 'BenchmarkTest00047' parameter from the query string, URL-decodes it, and directly passes it as the format string to `response.getWriter().format(param, obj)`. The result is written to the HTTP response without any HTML encoding or sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML or JavaScript by providing a malicious value in the query parameter. Additionally, line 71 sets 'X-XSS-Protection' to '0', which disables the browser's built-in XSS filter, making exploitation easier. No input validation or output encoding is applied to the reflected parameter.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via unescaped query string parameter
description: The servlet extracts a parameter value from the raw query string, URL-decodes it, and writes it directly to the HTTP response body within an HTML context. The response content type is set to 'text/html;charset=UTF-8', so the browser interprets the output as HTML. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript by crafting a malicious query parameter value (e.g., '?BenchmarkTest00048=<script>alert(1)</script>'). Additionally, the X-XSS-Protection header is explicitly disabled (set to '0'), removing a potential browser-level defense against reflected XSS. No output encoding, validation, or Content Security Policy is applied.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in query parameter value
description: The servlet sets the response content type to text/html, then extracts a parameter named 'BenchmarkTest00049' from the query string, URL-decodes it, and writes it directly into the response body without any HTML encoding or sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript by providing a malicious value for the parameter (e.g., <script>alert('XSS')</script>). Additionally, the X-XSS-Protection header is explicitly disabled (line 71), which removes a browser-level defense against reflected XSS.

title: Use of weak cryptographic algorithm (DES)
description: DES uses a 56-bit key, which is insufficient for modern security requirements and can be brute-forced in a short amount of time. The application uses DES to encrypt data, compromising confidentiality.

title: Information disclosure via stack traces in HTTP response
description: The application writes full stack traces to the HTTP response in error handling blocks. This exposes internal implementation details such as class names, file paths, and line numbers to the client, aiding attackers in understanding the application's internals and locating other vulnerabilities.

title: Command Injection via unsanitized user input in OS command execution
description: The parameter 'param' from the HTTP request is directly concatenated into a shell command string without any validation or sanitization. The command is executed using ProcessBuilder with '/c' (Windows) or '-c' (Unix), which passes the concatenated string to the shell. An attacker can inject arbitrary OS commands by including shell metacharacters (e.g., ';', '|', '&', '`', '$()') in the parameter value, leading to remote code execution.

title: SQL Injection in stored procedure call via string concatenation of user-controlled input
description: The parameter 'param' obtained from the HTTP request (line 46) is directly concatenated into a SQL stored procedure call string on line 48 without any sanitization or parameterization. Although prepareCall() is used, the SQL string is already fully constructed with user input before being passed to the database API. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL commands by providing malicious input in the 'BenchmarkTest00052' parameter, leading to SQL injection.

title: Use of DES (Data Encryption Standard) – weak, deprecated cryptographic algorithm
description: The code explicitly uses DES (Data Encryption Standard) for encryption in the doPost method. DES has a 56-bit key size, which is considered cryptographically broken and can be brute-forced in hours with modern hardware. This violates basic cryptographic strength requirements and exposes any encrypted data to decryption by attackers who obtain the ciphertext.

title: Cookie domain set from user-controlled Host header without validation
description: The cookie domain is derived from request.getRequestURL().toString(), which reflects the Host header sent by the client. An attacker can control the Host header (e.g. 'Host: attacker.com') to cause the server to set a cookie with Domain=attacker.com. If the browser accepts this cookie, the victim's browser could later send this cookie to the attacker-controlled domain, leading to cookie disclosure or session hijacking. The value is not validated or sanitized before being passed to setDomain().

title: Cookie path set from user-controlled request URI without sanitization
description: The cookie path is set directly from request.getRequestURI(), which is controlled by the client. An attacker can craft a request with an unusual URI (e.g., containing path traversal characters or very long path) to influence the cookie's scope. While browsers impose some restrictions on cookie paths, this can still lead to unexpected cookie scoping such as narrowing or widening the paths where the cookie is sent, potentially bypassing access controls.

title: Cookie domain set from user-controlled Host header allows cookie domain manipulation
description: The cookie domain is derived from the request URL's host, which is ultimately controlled by the Host header sent by the client. An attacker can send a request with a forged Host header, causing the server to set the cookie's domain attribute to an attacker-controlled domain. This can lead to the cookie being sent to unintended origins, enabling session hijacking or cookie theft if the victim visits the attacker's domain.

title: Cookie path set from user-controlled request URI
description: The cookie path is set directly from the request URI, which is supplied by the client. An attacker could potentially manipulate the request URI to set a broader path scope for the cookie, making the cookie accessible to other application paths. While the servlet container may normalize some traversal sequences, relying on user-controlled input for the path attribute weakens the cookie's intended scope restrictions.

title: Stack trace information exposed to client in error responses
description: In multiple catch blocks, the full stack trace of the exception is written directly to the response via `e.printStackTrace(response.getWriter())`. This exposes internal implementation details such as class names, method names, line numbers, and potentially file paths to the client. An attacker can use this information to better understand the application internals and craft further attacks.

title: Weak Cryptographic Algorithm (DES)
description: The code uses DES (Data Encryption Standard) which is a weak, deprecated algorithm with a 56-bit key size. DES is vulnerable to brute-force attacks and has been broken in practice. The use of DES exposes encrypted data to risk of decryption by attackers.

title: Information Exposure via Stack Traces
description: Multiple exception handlers call e.printStackTrace(response.getWriter()), which prints the full stack trace into the HTTP response sent to the client. This exposes internal implementation details such as class names, method names, file names, and line numbers, aiding attackers in crafting further attacks.

title: Sensitive Data Exposure in Response
description: The server echoes back the original plaintext input (bar) in the HTTP response after encryption. If the input contains sensitive data (e.g., from a cookie that may have been modified by an attacker), this leaks the value to anyone who can observe the response. Even though it is HTML-encoded, the plaintext is still exposed.

title: Cookie Domain Controlled by Request Host Header
description: The cookie domain is set to the hostname extracted from the request URL, which is derived from the Host header. If an attacker can control the Host header (e.g., when the application is behind a reverse proxy that does not validate it), they can set the cookie's domain to an arbitrary value. This could cause the cookie to be sent to unintended domains, leading to session leakage or cross-domain attacks.

title: Use of weak cryptographic algorithm DES
description: The code explicitly uses DES (Data Encryption Standard) for encryption. DES has a 56-bit key size, which is considered insecure due to its susceptibility to brute-force attacks. Modern hardware can break DES encryption in hours. The use of DES violates modern cryptographic standards and exposes encrypted data to recovery by attackers.

title: Information exposure via stack traces in HTTP response
description: In multiple catch blocks (lines 139, 145, 151, 157, 163, 169, 175), the exception stack trace is written directly to the HTTP response via response.getWriter(). This exposes internal implementation details such as class names, method names, file paths, and line numbers to the client. An attacker can use this information to refine further attacks against the application.

title: Cookie domain derived from user-controlled request host
description: The cookie domain is set by extracting the host from the request URL. An attacker who can control the Host header (e.g., via a crafted HTTP request) may cause the cookie to be set for an attacker-controlled domain. While the servlet container may validate the Host header to some extent, in many configurations or reverse-proxy setups the Host header is modifiable. This could facilitate cookie injection attacks where a cookie intended for the application is scoped to an attacker's domain.

title: Weak Cryptographic Algorithm: DES
description: The application uses DES (Data Encryption Standard), which has a 56-bit key size that can be brute-forced with modern hardware in a short amount of time. DES is deprecated and considered cryptographically broken. Both the cipher initialization on line 84 and the key generation on line 87 use DES. An attacker who obtains the encrypted output can decrypt it with modest computational resources, defeating the confidentiality protection this code intends to provide.

title: Use of CBC Mode Without Authentication (Padding Oracle Vulnerability)
description: The cipher is configured with CBC mode and PKCS5Padding. CBC mode does not provide integrity/authentication of the ciphertext. An attacker who can observe whether a padding error occurs (padding oracle) can decrypt the ciphertext by sending modified versions to the server. Because the encrypted result is stored in a file and the original input is reflected back in the response, the application could be susceptible to padding oracle attacks if the decryption path (not shown here) reveals padding failures.

title: Information Disclosure via Stack Trace in HTTP Response
description: When a cryptographic exception occurs, the full stack trace is written directly to the HTTP response via `response.getWriter()`. This exposes internal implementation details (class names, method names, line numbers, file paths) to the client. An attacker can use this information to learn about the application's internals, aiding in the development of further attacks.

title: Path traversal vulnerability via unsanitized cookie value used in file path construction
description: The value of the cookie "BenchmarkTest00060" is URL-decoded and used directly to construct a java.io.File without any validation or sanitization. An attacker can supply path traversal sequences (e.g., "../../etc/passwd") in the cookie value, allowing the construction of file paths outside the intended TESTFILES_DIR directory. Although the code does not read or write the file, it performs an existence check and exposes the resulting absolute path in the HTTP response (HTML-encoded). This leaks information about the server's file system and enables an attacker to probe for the existence of arbitrary files.

title: Host header injection leading to cookie domain manipulation
description: The cookie's Domain attribute is set directly from the host component of the request URL, which is derived from the Host header. An attacker who can control the Host header (e.g., through a proxy or misconfigured virtual hosting) can set the cookie's domain to an arbitrary value (e.g., an attacker-controlled domain). This could cause the browser to send the cookie to that domain, potentially leaking the cookie if it contained sensitive data. Although the cookie value in this specific code is hardcoded to "FileName", the vulnerability pattern is still present and could be exploited in similar code paths where the cookie carries sensitive data.

title: Path traversal via cookie-controlled file path
description: In the doPost method, the parameter 'param' is obtained directly from a cookie value (attacker-controlled) after URL decoding. This value is then Base64 encode/decoded (which is a no-op round-trip) and used as the parent path in a java.io.File constructor: new java.io.File(bar, "/Test.txt"). No validation or sanitization is performed on the path. An attacker can supply a value such as '../../' or an absolute path to traverse outside the intended directory. Although the code only checks file existence, this allows an attacker to probe for arbitrary files on the server filesystem, leading to information disclosure about the presence and location of sensitive files.

title: Cookie domain set from unvalidated Host header
description: In the doGet method, the cookie domain is set to the host extracted from the request URL, which is derived from the Host header. If an attacker can control the Host header (e.g., through HTTP Host header injection), they can set the cookie domain to an arbitrary domain. This could cause the cookie to be sent to a different domain, potentially leading to session hijacking or cookie disclosure if the cookie contained sensitive information. While the cookie value in this example is hardcoded and non-sensitive, the pattern is insecure and could be exploited if the cookie value were later changed to include a session identifier or token.

title: Path Traversal in File Read Operation
description: The 'bar' variable is derived from a cookie value controlled by the attacker (line 60, URL-decoded). It is concatenated directly with TESTFILES_DIR to form a file path (line 77) and then opened via FileInputStream (line 78). There is no validation or sanitization of the input to prevent path traversal sequences such as '../'. An attacker can manipulate the cookie to read arbitrary files on the server filesystem, leading to unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information.

title: Information Disclosure via Exception Messages
description: When an exception occurs while opening the file, the exception message is included in the HTTP response (after HTML encoding). The message may contain internal file paths, system details, or stack traces that could assist an attacker in further attacks. Although the output is HTML-encoded (preventing XSS), information leakage can still aid in reconnaissance.

title: Host Header Injection in Cookie Domain
description: The cookie domain is set using the host component of the request URL, which is derived from the client-supplied Host header. An attacker can manipulate the Host header (e.g., 'Host: attacker.com') to make the server set a cookie with a domain of 'attacker.com'. If the cookie contained sensitive data (session token), it could be exfiltrated to the attacker's domain. In this specific code the cookie value is hardcoded and not sensitive, but the pattern is still vulnerable and could be exploited in similar code paths.

title: Path Traversal (CWE-22) via cookie-controlled file path
description: The 'param' value originates directly from a request cookie (line 60), which is fully controlled by the client. The value is URL-decoded and then passed through a Base64 round-trip (lines 69-72) that does not alter the original bytes. The resulting 'bar' string (line 75) is concatenated directly into a file path without any validation, sanitization, or canonicalization. An attacker can supply a cookie value containing path traversal sequences (e.g., '../', '..\', or absolute paths like '/etc/passwd') to read arbitrary files on the server filesystem outside the intended TESTFILES_DIR directory.

title: Cookie domain set from unvalidated request URL (CWE-807 / CWE-644)
description: The cookie domain is set using the Host extracted from request.getRequestURL(). An attacker can manipulate the Host header in the HTTP request, which would cause the cookie to be set with an attacker-controlled domain. Although modern browsers enforce domain restrictions (cookies cannot be set for a different domain than the origin), a vulnerability in the URL parsing or proxy configuration could still allow setting a cookie for a parent or alternative domain, potentially leading to session fixation or cross-domain cookie injection.

title: Weak random number generator used for remember-me token
description: The code uses java.lang.Math.random() to generate a 'rememberMeKey' that is stored in a cookie and the session attribute to authenticate returning users. Math.random() relies on a linear congruential generator (LCG) which is not cryptographically secure. An attacker who can observe or predict the seed (e.g., by making multiple requests or knowing the approximate time of server startup) can predict future tokens and hijack user sessions. This undermines the authentication mechanism.

title: Potential HTTP response splitting via cookie domain attribute
description: The cookie's Domain attribute is set using the hostname extracted from the request URL (derived from the HTTP Host header). If an attacker can control the Host header (e.g., through a reverse proxy misconfiguration or direct network access), they could inject CRLF characters into the domain value. This could result in HTTP response splitting, allowing the attacker to inject additional headers or set cookies for arbitrary domains, bypassing security restrictions.

title: Potential HTTP response splitting via cookie path attribute
description: The cookie's Path attribute is set directly from the request URI, which is user-controllable. An attacker could craft a request URI containing CRLF sequences to perform HTTP response splitting, potentially injecting malicious cookies or headers. While many servlet containers reject such characters, the code does not perform any validation or sanitization, making it potentially exploitable in certain configurations.

title: OS Command Injection via unsanitized cookie value
description: The cookie value (param), which is attacker-controlled and URL-decoded, flows through the switch statement into the variable 'bar' (since guess.charAt(2) is always 'C', the switch assigns param to bar). This unsanitized string is concatenated directly into the shell command "echo " + bar on line 97. The command is executed via ProcessBuilder using cmd.exe /c or sh -c, which invokes a system shell. An attacker can inject arbitrary OS commands by including shell metacharacters (;, &&, |, backticks, etc.) in the cookie value, leading to full remote command execution on the server.

title: Use of weak random number generator (java.util.Random) for security-sensitive remember-me token
description: The remember-me token used for automatic authentication is generated using java.util.Random, which is a predictable linear congruential generator (LCG). An attacker who observes a few tokens can predict future tokens, allowing session hijacking. Additionally, the token is truncated to the fractional part of a float (approx. 7 decimal digits), reducing entropy to about 23 bits, which is brute-forceable.

title: Cookie domain derived from user-controlled Host header (request URL) enabling potential cookie injection
description: The cookie domain is set to the host extracted from the request URL, which is directly influenced by the HTTP Host header. If an attacker can control the Host header (e.g., by sending a request with a malicious Host value or through a proxy misconfiguration), the server will set a cookie for the attacker-controlled domain. This can lead to cookie injection across domains, enabling session fixation, session hijacking, or bypass of CSRF protections.

title: Information exposure of remember-me authentication token in HTTP response body
description: The remember-me token (which serves as an authentication credential) is printed directly into the HTML response. This exposes the token to anyone who can view the response (e.g., network observers, proxies, browser history, server logs, or any XSS victim). An attacker who obtains this token can impersonate the user without needing to know their password.

title: Weak random number generator used for security-sensitive authentication token
description: The remember-me authentication token (lines 69-70, 97-104) is generated using java.util.Random, which is a predictable linear congruential generator (LCG). Its internal state can be recovered after observing a few outputs, allowing an attacker to predict past or future tokens. Additionally, the token is later used at line 87 as the sole credential to re-authenticate a returning user via cookie. Using a cryptographically weak PRNG for authentication tokens violates basic security practices.

title: Insufficient entropy in authentication token (only 99 possible values)
description: The token space is limited to integers in the range [0, 98], i.e., only 99 possible values. An attacker can trivially enumerate all possibilities and forge a valid remember-me cookie. Even if the random number generator were cryptographically secure, this extremely small key space makes brute-force attacks trivial.

title: Cookie domain set from user-controlled Host header
description: The cookie domain is derived from request.getRequestURL().getHost(), which is influenced by the Host header sent by the client. If an attacker can control the Host header (e.g., through a reverse proxy that doesn't validate it), they could cause the cookie to be set for an arbitrary domain, potentially leaking the cookie to a different origin or enabling cookie injection attacks. Although modern browsers enforce domain-origin matching, older browsers or misconfigured proxies may honor the attacker-controlled domain.

title: Cookie path set from user-controlled request URI
description: The cookie path is set using request.getRequestURI(), which reflects the path portion of the request URL. An attacker who can craft a request with a manipulated URI (e.g., through path traversal or encoded characters) could influence the cookie's path attribute, potentially making the cookie accessible to a broader or unintended set of application paths. While the impact is limited compared to domain manipulation, it can still weaken cookie scoping.
